name: measured-noisy
title: Measured: fires more on human prose
description: Rules that hit human prose more often than AI prose on the audit corpus. Not wrong, and not removed from their original sets: a worn phrase is worth flagging whoever wrote it. But they are weak evidence about authorship and this set exists to say so in one place.

rules.name: Em dash
rules.description: An em dash, or an en dash or double hyphen standing in for one. Every occurrence, no threshold.
rules.suggest: A comma if the aside is light, a colon if what follows explains, brackets if it is a true aside, a full stop if it is really a second sentence.
rules.measured: This rule is a style preference, deliberately kept separate from the detection research. Four independent measurements agree the em dash does NOT distinguish machine prose from human prose: sloptells found acclaimed human writing uses more of them than models do (0.67 against 0.56 per 1000 characters); The Economist found only Claude above the human rate, with ChatGPT markedly below; humanizer-de states that a single em dash proves nothing; and this project's own corpus agreed. None of that is an argument for keeping them in your own writing, which is a different question and yours to answer.

hit: The migration took a week — longer than anyone expected.

rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 40 hits in 8/18 human documents, 0 in 0/18 AI documents.

rules.name: Echoing sentence runs
rules.description: Consecutive sentences built on the same repeated skeleton — “A shopping cart is an object in the system. A chat room is an object in the system.” The badge counts the echoing sentences.
rules.suggest: Merge the parallel sentences into one, or vary the structure.
rules.note: Known to fire on human prose. In an audit over 18 pre-2022 human documents it hit 10 of them and only 1 of 18 AI documents, because the shared run is usually the document's topic rather than a repeated frame: "the person who died" in guidance, "in the python 2" in a PEP. Kept unchanged because it is upstream's rule and the shape it describes is real. Tighter formulations are measured in candidates/variants.json and the numbers are in research/audit.md.

rules.name: “Turns out …”
rules.description: The casual-revelation opener, almost always bolted to a tidy conclusion: “Turns out X”, “it turns out that X”.
rules.suggest: State the finding without the casual-reveal framing.

hit: Turns out the cache was never warm.
It turns out that nobody tested it.
miss: She turns out solid work every week.

rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 1 hit in 1/18 human documents, 0 in 0/18 AI documents.

rules.name: Stacked rhetorical questions
rules.description: Two or more questions fired in a row, usually fragments after the first: “Do I know how it works? Where it breaks? Which corners it cut?” The badge counts the questions.
rules.suggest: Keep one question, or convert them to statements.
rules.note: Fires on essayists setting up a topic, which is a rhetorical move much older than the technology it is meant to detect: "Who are the speakers of AAE? How are they viewed?". Hit 3 of 18 human documents and 0 of 18 AI ones in the audit. Kept unchanged; stacked-questions-run3 in candidates/variants.json requires three in a row and removed every false positive.

hit: Do I know how it works? Where it breaks? Which corners it cut?
Was it worth it? Would I do it again?
miss: Did it work? Yes, and then some.

rules.name: Repeated sentence openers
rules.description: Three or more consecutive sentences starting on the same word — “Maybe nobody needed it. Maybe it introduced … Maybe a small convenience …” Pronouns and articles are ignored. The badge counts the sentences.
rules.suggest: Vary the sentence openings or combine into one sentence.

rules.name: Participle sentence tails
rules.description: Superficial analysis bolted onto a sentence end: “…, highlighting / underscoring / showcasing / reflecting the …”.
rules.suggest: End the sentence. The participle tail adds commentary, not information.

hit: The bridge reopened in June, highlighting the city’s investment in infrastructure.
Sales doubled, underscoring the strength of the brand.
miss: She kept highlighting passages in yellow.
The team, reflecting on the loss, regrouped.

rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 1 hit in 1/18 human documents, 0 in 0/18 AI documents.

rules.name: Stock essay metaphors
rules.description: The fixed stock of metaphors that essay-shaped generation reaches for: double-edged sword, level playing field, virtuous cycle, driving force behind, one-size-fits-all.
rules.suggest: Drop the metaphor and state the mechanism, or find one that belongs to this subject.

hit: Automation is a double-edged sword.
The API levels the playing field for small teams.
This creates a virtuous cycle of trust.
There is no one-size-fits-all answer.
miss: He balanced the tray with one hand.
The sword was mounted above the fireplace.

rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 1 hit in 1/18 human documents, 0 in 0/18 AI documents.

rules.name: Sentences march in formation
rules.description: Sentence lengths that barely vary. humanizer-de measures this as stddev_mean_ratio and requires at least 0.4 in every register profile it ships; sloptells describes the same thing as sentences that march in formation. The badge is the coefficient of variation — standard deviation over mean sentence length.
rules.suggest: Cut one sentence in half and let another run long. Rhythm is what stops correct prose from reading as generated.
rules.note: Threshold taken from humanizer-de's own German profiles and checked against English: sixteen documents of human technical prose ranged from 0.49 to 1.54, so 0.4 sits below all of them. Nothing about a low score proves authorship; it says the prose is monotone.

hit: The worker reads each record from the queue and checks its schema. The schema lives in a shared repository that both teams can edit. A record that fails the check is written to a separate log. The log is rotated every night and kept for thirty days. An operator reviews the log each morning before the standup meeting. Most of the failures come from a single partner in the north. That partner has been sending malformed dates since the middle of March. We opened a ticket with their integration team on the same day. The ticket has not received a reply from anyone on their side. We now reject their malformed records at the edge of the system. The change was fifteen lines and shipped on a Tuesday afternoon. Nobody on the team noticed the change had gone out at all. The operator noticed because she stopped being paged at six each morning. She sent a short message to the channel to say so. That message has been pinned in the channel ever since that day. The queue has now run clean for four consecutive months without trouble. We have not touched the retry logic in any way since then. Eleven records are sitting in the dead letter queue this morning. All eleven of them came from the same partner in the north. We check the queue on Friday afternoons now instead of every day. The runbook still tells the operator to check it every single morning. Somebody on the team should update that page in the runbook. So far nobody has found the time to go and do it.
miss: Short. The worker reads each record from the queue and checks it against a schema that lives in a shared repository both teams can edit, which sounded sensible at the time and has since caused two outages. A record that fails is logged. The log rotates nightly. An operator reviews it each morning before standup, and most of what she finds comes from one partner in the north who has been sending malformed dates since March, a fact we established within an hour and have been unable to act on since. We opened a ticket. No reply. We now reject their malformed records at the edge instead, which took fifteen lines and shipped on a Tuesday afternoon with no announcement, no review beyond the usual one, and no ceremony of any kind. Nobody noticed. The operator noticed, because she stopped being paged at six, and she sent a two-word message to the channel that has been pinned there ever since and remains the only recognition that change will ever get. Four months clean. The retry logic is untouched. Eleven records sit in the dead letter queue this morning, all from the same partner, and we check on Fridays now rather than daily even though the runbook, which nobody has updated, still says every morning. Somebody should fix that. Nobody will. The wider lesson, if there is one, is that the smallest change on the board turned out to be the one that mattered, and that the person who noticed was the only person the system had actually been hurting all along, which is roughly how these things go everywhere I have worked. Four months. No pages. Nobody asked.

rules.name: Negation then correction, across a sentence break
rules.description: "X isn't A. It's B." — the correction split over two sentences, so a within-sentence rule misses it.
rules.suggest: Say what it is. The denial adds nothing the assertion does not.
